title: Requirements Gathering
description: Learn how to collect, validate, and prioritize system requirements. Master stakeholder interviews, user stories, acceptance criteria, and the MoSCoW method to build a solid foundation for any system design.

data.text: Every well-designed system starts with clear requirements. As a senior engineer, you will often lead the conversation with stakeholders who may not know exactly what they need. Your job is to ask the right questions, uncover hidden constraints, and translate business goals into technical specifications that your team can build.

Requirements gathering is not a one-time checklist. It is an ongoing conversation that continues through design, implementation, and launch. Getting it wrong early means rebuilding later — often at great cost.

Functional requirements describe what the system should do. Non-functional requirements describe how well it should do it. Both are equally important, but teams often overlook non-functional requirements until performance problems appear in production.

data.title: Functional Requirements Examples
items: Users can upload a profile photo
The system sends a confirmation email after checkout
Admins can export sales reports as CSV

data.title: Non-Functional Requirements Examples
items: The checkout page loads in under 2 seconds for 95% of users
The system supports 10,000 concurrent checkout requests
Data is replicated across two availability zones with zero loss

data.title: Common Mistake
data.text: Teams often treat non-functional requirements as optional. They are not. Latency, availability, and data durability requirements shape every major architectural decision.

Stakeholders include product managers, end users, operations teams, legal or compliance teams, and sometimes customers. Each group sees the system from a different angle. A product manager wants features. An operations team wants observability. A compliance team wants audit trails.

data.title: Interview Preparation Steps
items: List every stakeholder group that will be affected by the system
Prepare open-ended questions for each group
Schedule short, focused sessions — 30 to 45 minutes each
Record (with permission) or take detailed notes

data.text: User stories capture a requirement from the user's perspective. The classic format is: "As a [role], I want [feature], so that [benefit]." Acceptance criteria define the conditions under which the story is considered complete.

data.title: User Story Example
data.content: As a customer, I want to save items to a wishlist so that I can purchase them later.
data.code:
Acceptance Criteria:
1. User can add any product to their wishlist from the product page
2. User can view all wishlist items in one place
3. User can remove items from the wishlist
4. Wishlist persists across sessions
5. Maximum 100 items per wishlist

data.text: Not all requirements can be delivered at once. The MoSCoW method forces you to sort requirements into four categories: Must have, Should have, Could have, and Won't have. This creates a realistic roadmap and protects the team from scope creep.

rows: Critical for launch. Without it, the release fails.
User authentication and secure session handling
Important but not critical for the first release.
Desirable but can be deferred to a later release.
Explicitly out of scope for this release.

data.text: Traceability links each requirement to its origin, design decision, implementation, and test case. When a requirement changes, traceability tells you exactly what needs to be updated. Without it, changes become a guessing game that risks breaking unrelated features.

data.title: Pro Tip
data.text: Use a simple spreadsheet or a requirements management tool to track requirement IDs, descriptions, source stakeholders, priority, and current status. Update it after every design review.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Functional requirements define what the system does; non-functional requirements define how well it performs
Interview every stakeholder group to uncover hidden constraints and conflicting priorities
User stories and acceptance criteria translate vague needs into testable conditions
MoSCoW prioritization protects the team from scope creep
Traceability ensures that changes ripple through the system safely
data.takeaway: Good requirements gathering prevents expensive redesigns later. Invest time here.

items.question: What is the difference between a requirement and a wish?
items.answer: A requirement is something the system must do to meet a business or user need. A wish is something someone would like but that is not essential. The MoSCoW method helps you tell them apart.

items.question: How many stakeholder interviews should I conduct?
items.answer: Aim for 5 to 12 interviews for a medium-sized project. Fewer than five risks missing perspectives; more than twelve becomes difficult to synthesize.

items.question: Can requirements change after the design phase starts?
items.answer: Yes, and they will. The goal is to minimize changes after launch, not to freeze requirements entirely. Build traceability so you can assess the impact of each change quickly.

data.title: Interview Simulation: Online Bookstore
data.description: You are designing an online bookstore. Interview three personas: a customer, a store manager, and a warehouse worker. Write at least two user stories and two acceptance criteria for each persona.
data.expectedOutcome: A set of six user stories with clear acceptance criteria, each tagged with a MoSCoW priority.
